analysis.one_liner: Requires big political spenders to name their top donors and closes foreign-money loopholes in elections.
analysis.headline: A campaign-transparency bill backed by 189 House Democrats and no Republicans has sat in three House committees with no action since its March 2026 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The DISCLOSE Act would require corporations, unions, super PACs, and nonprofits that spend more than $10,000 influencing federal elections to report that spending to the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours, and to name the largest donors behind it. Ads would have to carry a 'stand by every ad' statement naming the top funders who paid for them. It also tightens the ban on foreign money by covering digital ads, ballot initiatives, and shell companies used to hide a foreign donor's identity, with criminal penalties of up to five years. It was referred to three House committees and has seen no action since.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would learn within a day who is paying for the political ads they see, including the top five funders behind each ad. Candidates and groups targeted by anonymous attack ads would gain a way to show voters who is behind them, and enforcers would get new tools against foreign money in elections.

how_it_helps.text: Covered organizations spending over $10,000 on elections must report each campaign-related disbursement over $1,000 to the FEC within 24 hours, under penalty of perjury.

Ads paid for with disclosed spending must carry a statement from the CEO or top official approving the message, plus a list of the organization's top five funders (top two for audio ads), or a link to that list for very short ads.

The foreign-money ban is extended to paid digital ads, electioneering communications, ballot initiatives and referenda for covered foreign nationals, and communications about federal judicial nominations.
Establishing or using a corporation or shell entity to conceal a foreign national's election contribution becomes a federal crime carrying up to five years in prison.
The GAO must study and report each four-year cycle on illicit foreign money in federal elections, including which communities it targeted.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, labor unions, 501(c) nonprofits, and super PACs that spend on elections would bear new 24-hour reporting, recordkeeping, and per-ad disclaimer duties. Large digital platforms would handle expanded ad-disclaimer requirements. The people behind dark-money groups would lose the ability to fund election ads without their names attached.

drawbacks.text: Naming top funders on every ad and filing within 24 hours exposes donors' political ties; the bill answers this with a harassment exemption that requires 'specific and particular evidence' of serious threats and is subject to FEC rules, but critics argue the standard and the four-year reapplication burden still chill participation and add paperwork.
The reporting and disclaimer duties fall on corporations, labor unions, and nonprofits alike, and organizations near the $10,000 threshold face compliance costs disproportionate to their spending.

Some political spending routes through ordinary business income, which the bill expressly exempts from disclosure, so a well-advised spender can still keep much of its funding profile out of public view.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency gains are large and targeted: the same ad would still run, but voters would see who paid for it, and hidden foreign money would face criminal exposure. The costs are real but manageable for large spenders — the bill sets a $10,000 floor, exempts ordinary commercial transactions, and provides a harassment exemption — though small groups near the threshold and high-volume digital advertisers would feel the paperwork. The bill's own findings invoke the Supreme Court's description of disclosure as the less restrictive alternative to limiting spending outright.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three House committees, and no committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Pappas introduced the bill on March 4, 2026, joined by 188 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans.
It was referred to the House Administration, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees simultaneously, which splits the bill's fate across three committees.
The action history shows only the introduction and the referral; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action has occurred.
Past versions of the DISCLOSE Act advanced only with Democratic control and repeatedly stalled in the Senate, where 60 votes are needed to move past a filibuster.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Undisclosed political spenders — super PACs, dark-money nonprofits, and corporations funding election ads — remain better off with the bill stalled, since nothing requires them to reveal their donors. Foreign-money enforcement also remains as it was, without the new digital and ballot-initiative rules.

sides.party_line_note: All 189 initial supporters were House Democrats, and no Republican has cosponsored, in a chamber where Republicans hold 223 of 441 seats.

industries.note: Their operating model depends on spending unlimited money without naming donors. The bill would force 24-hour FEC reporting of election spending over $10,000 and disclosure of beneficial owners and large funders, ending the anonymity these groups rely on.

Corporations that fund election ads would have to report each disbursement over $1,000, list beneficial owners, and have the CEO approve each ad by name. Ordinary commercial income is exempt, but political spending would no longer be traceable-free.

Platforms with 50 million or more U.S. monthly visitors would face expanded disclaimer duties on political ads, including funder lists or links, adding compliance work but also a uniform federal rule for political ad sales.

Unions are covered organizations and would bear the same 24-hour reporting and disbursement disclosure as corporations, though dues-based transfers between affiliates get special treatment. Unions generally favor disclosure of corporate dark money even while absorbing their own reporting costs.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican House majority, zero Republican cosponsors, and a three-way committee referral that has produced no hearings or markup, the bill is unlikely to reach the House floor this Congress. Even if it did, a Senate version would need 60 votes to clear a filibuster in a 55-45 Republican Senate, which no comparable disclosure bill has achieved.
